payload.rationale: To resolve as YES, the 2026 annual anomaly must be strictly greater than 1.28 C (since 1.28 C is higher than the 2025 value of 1.19 C). The sum of the anomalies for the first 8 months of 2026 is 9.79 C (averaging ~1.224 C). For the annual average to exceed 1.28 C, the total sum for the 12 months must exceed 15.36 C. This means the remaining 4 months (September-December) must sum to more than 5.57 C, which requires an average of >1.393 C per month. So far in 2026, only August (1.40 C) has exceeded this required average. The strongest reason this estimate could be too low is if a strong El Niño or other rapid warming event is currently intensifying, which could push late-year anomalies consistently above 1.40 C. The strongest reason it could be too high is that achieving an average of ~1.39 C over four consecutive months represents a massive and sustained jump from the 1.22 C average observed over the first two-thirds of the year, making the required threshold nearly mathematically out of reach under normal variance.
limitations: No ENSO forecast or current ENSO state is provided to gauge late-year temperature trends.
Only 8 months of data are available, leaving one-third of the year unknown.
Monthly anomalies can be volatile, and historical context for late-year spikes is not provided.
